notes.b: Foreign direct investment (FDI) is money a company puts into another country in a way that gives it a lasting interest in, and a degree of control over, a business or asset there. Governments compete for it because it brings jobs, tax and skills, so you need to be able to define it and tell its forms apart.
points: Definition: FDI is investment by a company in one country that creates a lasting interest and some control over a business or asset in another country. For example, a sample US technology firm builds an office in Dublin and runs it as part of its own group.

FDI differs from portfolio investment, which means buying shares or bonds without seeking managerial control. A fund that buys a few shares in an Irish company is a portfolio investor, because it has no say in how the firm is run.
Greenfield investment builds new facilities from the ground up, such as a factory or office, which adds new productive capacity to the host country.

Acquisition, sometimes called brownfield investment, buys an existing business or site. Ownership transfers to the foreign firm, but no new capacity is added at once because the business already existed.
A multinational enterprise owns or controls operations in more than one country, and most FDI is made by multinationals.

FDI is usually a long-term commitment, because building or buying a business abroad is costly to reverse. This is why it tends to be less volatile than portfolio flows, which can be sold quickly. It is not always permanent, since firms can leave.
This subsection is about inward FDI, meaning foreign firms investing in Ireland. It does not cover Irish firms investing abroad (outward FDI).
notes.tip: Keep the confusable pairs clear: FDI has lasting interest and control, portfolio investment has none; greenfield is new, acquisition is existing. To explain FDI at the depth an exam expects, give the definition, one example and why countries compete for it.

notes.h: How Ireland attracts FDI: IDA Ireland
notes.b: Ireland does not leave FDI to chance. A state agency actively promotes the country to foreign firms, and this is how the government promotes FDI.
points: IDA Ireland is the state agency responsible for attracting and supporting foreign investment in manufacturing and internationally traded services (services sold to customers abroad).

It promotes Ireland overseas, offers grants and supports, helps firms find sites and property, and connects them with skills providers, so a firm considering Ireland can get help from first enquiry to opening.
IDA Ireland attracts foreign firms. Enterprise Ireland is a different agency that helps Irish firms to export, so the two must not be swapped.

IDA reported a record 323 investments in 2025, a 38 per cent rise on 2024 (announced 18 December 2025). Its 2025 annual report records a net rise of 4,726 jobs in client companies, bringing direct employment in client companies to 312,468, about 11 per cent of national employment.
notes.tip: To answer how the government promotes FDI, name IDA Ireland, say what it does, and give at least two of the four factors the specification names: human capital development, pro-enterprise policy, access to markets and research. Do not give a number of jobs promised, because reports differ.

notes.h: Why firms choose Ireland: skills, policy, markets and research
notes.b: IDA Ireland can only promote what Ireland actually offers. A firm deciding where to locate weighs the quality of the workforce, the rules, the customers it can reach and the research base, and each of these is a reason Ireland can point to.
points: Human capital development: human capital is the competencies embodied in people, invested in, and developed to help them to be more productive and realise their potential. Ireland offers an educated, English-speaking workforce, built through third-level institutions and further education and training bodies such as SOLAS.
SOLAS is the state agency responsible for further education and training in Ireland, so it helps supply the skilled workers that foreign firms need to recruit.

Pro-enterprise policy: a stable legal and regulatory framework gives foreign firms the confidence to invest for the long term, because they can plan for years ahead without fearing sudden rule changes.

Access to markets: EU membership gives access to the single market (the EU countries trading as one market) without tariffs, and Ireland has a network of trade agreements. A firm based here can sell across the EU without tariffs at borders.

Research: universities and research centres, together with state research funding through Research Ireland, attract research and development (R&D) investment because firms can work alongside researchers and recruit graduates.

Clusters: related firms concentrated in one area, such as ICT firms in Dublin and pharmaceutical and medical technology firms in Cork, Limerick and Galway, draw in further investment and specialist suppliers. A new firm in a cluster finds suppliers and skilled staff already nearby.
notes.tip: When asked for two reasons a firm would locate in Ireland, give two different reasons and link each to the firm's decision, for example the English-speaking workforce lets it recruit easily. A common mistake is writing low tax alone, or giving two reasons that are really the same.

notes.h: Corporation tax and the global minimum tax
notes.b: Corporation tax is part of Ireland's FDI offer, but international agreement is narrowing the gap between countries' tax rates for the largest groups.
points: Corporation tax is a tax on company profits, and Ireland's rate is 12.5 per cent on trading income. It is different from income tax, which is paid by individuals.

The OECD global minimum tax, known as Pillar Two, sets a 15 per cent minimum effective tax rate for groups with consolidated revenue (combined revenue of the whole group) of at least 750 million euro in two of the four preceding years.
Ireland began applying the Pillar Two rules from 31 December 2023. Most companies in Ireland are outside their scope, because only very large groups meet the revenue threshold.
Pillar Two reduces the advantage of a low tax rate for the largest groups, so Ireland's appeal rests more on non-tax factors such as skills and infrastructure.
Tax policy for multinationals is shaped by OECD and EU agreements as well as by Irish law, so changes can come from international agreement rather than from the Irish government alone.

Ethical angle: the global minimum tax aims to limit competition between countries on tax, which supports tax fairness, since large groups cannot pay very little tax simply by choosing the lowest-tax country.
notes.tip: Always give the threshold when you mention the global minimum tax, because it applies only to very large groups. Linking the tax to the firm's choice, not just stating low tax, is what a developed answer does.

notes.b: FDI brings direct and indirect benefits to the Irish economy, although their size and spread vary. Each opportunity is stronger when you explain its effect on the economy, public finances or communities.
points: Employment: foreign firms employ many workers directly, and their suppliers and service providers create further indirect jobs, which raises incomes and spending in local economies.
Revenue: corporation tax paid by multinationals funds public services, and their employees pay income tax and the Universal Social Charge, so the state has more to spend on health and education.
Research and development and innovation: multinationals invest in R&D centres in Ireland, supporting innovation and high-skilled jobs.
Skills transfer: employees trained by multinationals can move to Irish firms and spread technical and management skills, so the benefit continues after the foreign firm's own staff leave.
Supplier linkages: multinationals buy goods and services from local firms, which can help Irish SMEs (small and medium-sized enterprises) grow.
Regional development: FDI in regional towns and cities outside Dublin creates jobs beyond the capital.
Infrastructure: investment can support demands for better transport, utilities and digital infrastructure, although the same growth also puts pressure on what already exists.
Digital angle: much FDI in Ireland is in ICT, digital services and data centres, so digital technology firms bring skills and innovation.
notes.tip: Pair every opportunity with a limit. Outline two opportunities and give each its effect, because naming jobs and tax alone with no effect is a common mistake. To link to current events, IDA's record 2025 results show how FDI wins create jobs, but the news is only as reliable as what the figures count.

notes.b: The benefits of FDI depend on how Ireland manages dependence on a few firms, housing, infrastructure and the links to the domestic economy. When you outline a challenge, always explain its effect.
points: Concentration: a few large firms provide a large share of corporation tax receipts, which leaves public finances exposed if one firm leaves or its profits fall.
Footloose investment: firms can relocate if taxes, costs or regulation change, so Ireland must keep its offer competitive. This is why FDI is usually, not always, long term.

Pressure on housing and infrastructure: rapid job growth in Dublin increases demand for housing, transport and water, raising rents and congestion. This is an ethical issue as well as an economic one, because local people bear the cost.

Profit repatriation: profits paid to overseas parent companies leave the economy. This is why GNI* is used alongside GDP. GDP measures output within a country, but GNI* is a modified measure of national income published by the CSO to remove the distortion from globalised multinational activity.
GNI* is smaller than GDP, which shows that GDP overstates the income left in Ireland. You do not need to learn the figures.
Effect on Irish SMEs: multinationals compete for skilled staff and can push up wages, making it harder for SMEs to recruit.
Limited linkages: some multinationals buy most of their inputs abroad, so the benefit to local suppliers can be small.

Sustainability angle: data centres and large manufacturing sites have high energy and water demand, and digital technology firms add demand on the electricity grid. Firms may be expected to report on ESG (environmental, social and governance) factors.
notes.tip: Give challenges with their effects. Housing alone is a common mistake: link it to higher rents. Mention GNI* only to show that GDP overstates the income left in Ireland. Where asked to evaluate, bring in the ethical or sustainability angle, such as housing, energy demand or tax fairness.

notes.h: Analysing business news and forming an opinion
notes.b: In Applying my learning you are asked to analyse a business news story and give an informed opinion. That needs a clear method, not a general view.
points: 1. Identify the central claim in the news story, such as a new investment announcement or a change in tax policy. Restating the headline is not analysis.
2. Check the evidence: the number of jobs, the timescale, the amount invested, and whether the figures are announced or confirmed. Do not accept a headline figure without asking what it counts.
3. Identify the stakeholders affected, such as workers, local communities, suppliers, government and shareholders.
4. Weigh short-term and long-term effects: a new plant may create jobs quickly but may depend on future policy and tax rules.
5. Examine the story's assumptions and perspectives, because different groups can read the same event very differently.
6. Form a judgement, support it with at least two pieces of evidence, and state a limitation of your view.

Worked example: in December 2025 IDA Ireland reported record investment wins for 2025 despite US tariff uncertainty (irishtimes.com and rte.ie, 18 December 2025). The opportunity is jobs; the challenge is dependence on US-linked firms.
Practice story: pick a recent FDI story, such as a pharmaceutical or technology investment announcement, and check its details on a reputable news source before you use it.

Practice example: in January and February 2026 EU governments approved the EU-Mercosur trade agreement with Ireland voting against, and the Commission moved to apply it provisionally; Irish beef farmers' groups opposed it (irishtimes.com, 9 January and 27 February 2026). It has winners and losers, so it suits stakeholder analysis.
notes.tip: A full answer states the claim, checks the evidence, names stakeholders, weighs short and long term, gives a judgement supported by two pieces of evidence, and states a limit of the view. Do not invent figures. When using a company story, use only details you have checked on a reputable news source; for practice use a sample pharmaceutical firm announcing a new plant.

keyTerms.definition: Investment by a company in one country that creates a lasting interest and some control over a business or asset in another country.
Investment that builds new facilities from the ground up in another country.
Buying shares or bonds in a foreign company without seeking managerial control.
The state agency that attracts and supports foreign investment in manufacturing and internationally traded services.
The skills, knowledge and education of a country's workforce, which affects its productivity.
A tax levied on the profits of companies.
The transfer of profits earned in one country back to owners in another country.
Investment that can move to another country easily if costs, taxes or regulation change.

factCards.term: Four named attractions for FDI in Ireland
factCards.definition: Human capital development, pro-enterprise policy, access to markets and research.
Jobs, tax revenue, research and development, skills transfer and supplier linkages.
Concentrated tax receipts, footloose investment, pressure on housing and infrastructure, and profit repatriation.
Greenfield builds new capacity; acquisition transfers an existing business and its capacity.
A 15 per cent minimum effective tax rate for very large multinational groups under the OECD agreement.

factCards.term: Steps for analysing a business news story
factCards.definition: Identify the claim, check the evidence, identify stakeholders, weigh short and long-term effects, then give a supported opinion.

questions.prompt: Outline two reasons a multinational firm would choose to locate in Ireland.
questions.model: First, Ireland offers human capital: an educated, English-speaking workforce with graduates in science, technology and engineering, which lets a firm staff technical or customer-facing roles without relocating staff from abroad. Second, Ireland gives access to the EU single market, so a firm based here can sell to other member states without tariffs and serve EU customers from one base. Both reasons help a firm reduce its costs and manage its operations across Europe.

questions.prompt: Explain the term foreign direct investment, outline how the Irish government promotes it, and outline its contribution to the Irish economy.
questions.model: Foreign direct investment is investment by a company in one country that creates a lasting interest and some control over a business or asset in another country, such as building a factory or acquiring an existing firm. The government promotes FDI mainly through IDA Ireland, which markets Ireland overseas, offers grants and property, and helps firms find skilled staff. Ireland also offers a stable regulatory framework and a corporation tax rate of 12.5 per cent on trading income, which encourages long-term investment. FDI contributes to the economy through employment, tax revenue from corporation tax and employee income tax, investment in research and development, and skills transfer to Irish firms as employees move between companies.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the opportunities and challenges of FDI for Ireland, and give an informed opinion on whether Ireland should continue to rely heavily on FDI.
questions.model: The main opportunities are employment, both direct and indirect through suppliers, and tax revenue that funds public services. Multinationals also invest in research and development and transfer skills, and supplier linkages can help Irish SMEs grow. The challenges are that a small number of firms provide a large share of corporation tax, so public finances are exposed if one leaves, and footloose investment can move if tax or costs change. Rapid growth around Dublin adds pressure on housing and infrastructure, and profits paid abroad mean that GDP overstates the income that stays in the economy. My view is that Ireland should keep attracting FDI because its employment and skills benefits are substantial, but it should reduce dependence on a few firms by strengthening linkages with Irish SMEs and by investing in housing and infrastructure. The main limitation of this view is that the benefits are uneven across regions and sectors.
